rationale: B wins because it sees the most reportable hole in the update and makes it the story: “Hims & Hers won't say where its compounded semaglutide comes from.” A has real material, but it starts decorating the record with lines like “Novo Nordisk Spent Years Building the GLP-1 Market” and “Eli Lilly,” neither of which was supplied. B is tighter strategist work: sharper beats, fewer fantasy protagonists, harder proof gates, and the right warning before anyone pitches a product sitting under an FDA risk flag.
gaps_in_A: “Novo Nordisk Spent Years Building the GLP-1 Market” and “Eli Lilly” name specific manufacturers not supplied in the update. The facts only say branded manufacturers pushed back.
“clearest test case yet” and “entering the space at scale” overstate the launch. The update says Hims is public and launching access; it does not prove scale or uniqueness.
“Its First Big Move Carries FDA Risk” invents sequence and importance. The update says Hims recently turned profitable, not that this is its first major strategic move.
The unnamed supply source is treated mostly as “Proof it needs” instead of its own supply-chain/regulatory angle. That is probably the first story a serious reporter sees.
gaps_in_B: “Hims & Hers won't say where its compounded semaglutide comes from” overstates “not named” into refusal. Use “has not named” unless someone asked and got a no.
“prescription by video” is not in the facts. The update says telehealth visit; that could be synchronous video, async review, or both.
“putting compounded semaglutide at the center of a consumer offering” pushes beyond the record. The launch is real, but centrality and revenue importance need proof.

It refuses the bad affordability angles but loses the cleaner patient-access version. “A fraction of branded-drug prices” is weak without numbers, but it is still a usable consumer-health path if the price and a real patient exist.
